title: Unequal-bin histograms: make rectangle area carry frequency
summary: Compute density heights for unequal intervals, document edge inclusion and reconcile plotted area to the measured population.
body:
Compute density heights for unequal intervals, document edge inclusion and reconcile plotted area to the measured population.

Define the measured population before the bins

A histogram partitions a numerical measure into adjacent intervals. Each observation belongs to one interval, and the shape depends on the chosen boundaries. Specify the observation unit, measurement unit, eligibility window and treatment of missing values before drawing. A delivery-latency chart over requests differs from one over customers even if both use milliseconds on the horizontal axis. Fixed bin edges let readers compare weeks without interpreting a shifted boundary as a changed distribution. Do not silently trim values outside the visible domain; either expand the domain or label the excluded count and range. Grain and denominator choices come first, and outlier displays can preserve extreme values that a compact histogram hides.

For unequal widths, height is a density

When widths vary, raw counts cannot be the rectangle heights if the picture is supposed to preserve frequency. Divide each bin's count by its width for count density, or divide again by the total number of included observations for probability density. The rectangle area then equals its count or share. A 40-unit-wide bin containing two requests and an 80-unit-wide bin containing four requests have equal probability-density height, although the second contains twice as many requests. Print counts or shares on demand; height alone is easy to misread. State whether intervals are left-closed and right-open, and make the final upper boundary inclusive if that is the published rule. Axis integrity requires a labeled density unit, such as share per millisecond, rather than a mislabeled 'number of requests' vertical axis.

Choose edges without chasing the answer

A histogram with very wide bins buries local peaks. Very narrow bins turn sampling noise into apparent structure. Pick boundaries using measurement resolution and a declared analytical purpose, then inspect sensitivity using another reasonable fixed bin plan. Do not search many boundaries and publish only the one that makes a preferred group look unusual. For side-by-side cohorts, use shared edges and a shared vertical density scale; sample-size differences belong in annotations and raw-count tables. If an interval is open-ended, it has no finite width and cannot receive an ordinary density rectangle. Split it at a finite bound, or display its count separately. Shared-scale small multiples make the bin plan visible across groups.

Reconcile the chart before interpretation

The bin ledger should sum to the included record count. For a probability-density histogram, the sum of height times width should equal one apart from floating-point rounding. Those checks catch dropped boundary observations, double assignment and a denominator that includes records outside the plotted range. The code below rejects out-of-range measurements rather than making an attractive but incomplete chart. A separate report can show excluded or invalid records under a declared policy. Give readers an accessible interval table with bounds, counts, shares and density; a smooth overlay is a different estimate with its own bandwidth and should not erase the measured bins. Density bandwidth and text alternatives cover those follow-on decisions.

Worked contract

from bisect import bisect_right
from math import isfinite

def histogram_ledger(latencies_ms: list[float], edges_ms: list[float]):
    if (not latencies_ms or len(edges_ms) < 2 or
            any(not isfinite(edge) for edge in edges_ms) or
            any(left >= right for left, right in zip(edges_ms, edges_ms[1:]))):
        raise ValueError("supply observations and strictly increasing finite edges")
    counts = [0] * (len(edges_ms) - 1)
    for latency in latencies_ms:
        if not isfinite(latency) or latency < edges_ms[0] or latency > edges_ms[-1]:
            raise ValueError("every observation must be finite and inside the domain")
        index = min(bisect_right(edges_ms, latency) - 1, len(counts) - 1)
        counts[index] += 1
    total = len(latencies_ms)
    ledger = [(left, right, count, count / total,
               count / (total * (right - left)))
              for left, right, count in zip(edges_ms, edges_ms[1:], counts)]
    assert sum(row[2] for row in ledger) == total
    assert abs(sum((row[1] - row[0]) * row[4] for row in ledger) - 1) < 1e-12
    return ledger

request_latencies = [47, 59, 83, 97, 131, 149, 173, 211, 227, 251]
bins = histogram_ledger(request_latencies, [40, 80, 160, 320])
assert [row[2] for row in bins] == [2, 4, 4]
assert bins[0][4] == bins[1][4] == 0.005
assert histogram_ledger([40, 80, 160, 320], [40, 80, 160, 320])[-1][2] == 2

Performance and operating cost

For N measurements and B bins, binary search assigns each observation in O(log B) time, so the sweep costs O(N log B); constructing the ledger costs O(B). The returned counts and rows need O(B) extra space. The ten-request check gives bin shares 0.2, 0.4 and 0.4, while the first two densities both equal 0.005 share per millisecond. The boundary assertion places 80 in the second interval and includes 320 in the final interval. Preserve this boundary policy when computing comparison charts.

Common Mistakes

  • Using raw counts as rectangle heights when widths differ.
  • Labeling a probability-density vertical axis as a count axis.
  • Dropping the last-edge observation or assigning an internal edge twice.
  • Changing bin boundaries between cohorts and reading the changed geometry as changed behavior.

Validation drill

Measure 470 request latencies, declare three unequal finite intervals and audit every boundary value. Publish an interval ledger, an excluded-record count, a fixed-edge comparison for a second week and a density-area check that equals one.

title: Cohort retention heatmaps: keep immature cells blank
summary: Fix first-entry membership, define the return event and reserve zero for a mature period with no returning members.
body:
Fix first-entry membership, define the return event and reserve zero for a mature period with no returning members.

Anchor each member once

A cohort retention heatmap groups entities by a first qualifying period, then shows the share that performs a specified return action at each elapsed age. Rows are entry cohorts; columns are ages, not calendar dates. The entity might be a user, account or device, and those IDs are not interchangeable. Deduplicate signup records, resolve identity before grouping and keep each member in the original cohort. If a person returns after an inactive week, they still belong to their first cohort. Choose the return event precisely: opening the app, completing a project and making a payment yield different retention curves. Grain and denominator rules prevent an event count from masquerading as a user count. Funnels answer a related but different progression question.

Hold the original denominator fixed

In return-in-period retention, the numerator at age three is the number of original cohort members active in that period; the denominator is the size of that original eligible cohort. Do not divide by last week's active members unless the chart explicitly measures conditional continuation. Several return events by one member in the same period count once. An age-zero cell is one only if it represents enrollment by definition; it is not automatically one when age zero requires a distinct return action. State whether the chart means activity in that exact period, any activity up to that period, or continuous activity in every period. Those definitions can reverse the visual impression. Linked filters must recalculate cohort membership and denominator together rather than filtering only the numerator.

Separate zero from not yet observed

A young cohort has not reached later ages. Its future cells are undefined, not zero percent. A mature cohort with no returning member has a genuine zero. The current partial week is another state: until it closes, all cohorts' cells for that calendar week are provisional, because an apparent decline can simply be missing future activity. Keep a last-complete-period watermark, emit blank cells beyond it and label the watermark on the display. The triangular blank region should use a distinct missing pattern or text, not the low-retention color. Older data can still be incomplete because event ingestion is delayed; an as-of timestamp and an ingestion-lag audit should accompany published comparisons. Heatmap missingness and period completeness provide the display contract.

Compare equal ages and adequate support

Reading down one age column compares groups at the same lifecycle point; reading diagonally compares the same calendar period across groups of different ages. The latter can reveal a platform outage, but it is not a direct retention comparison. Show cohort sizes because 50 percent may represent one of two members or 5,000 of 10,000. Keep one zero-to-one color range across all rows and do not stretch each row independently. For small cohorts, add counts or uncertainty intervals and avoid strong claims from a bright cell. Segment-specific charts need an eligibility rule frozen at entry; defining a segment using future behavior leaks outcomes into cohort assignment. Small-sample display and calendar completeness help audit this comparison.

Worked contract

from collections import defaultdict

def retention_ledger(enrollments: list[tuple[str, int]],
                     return_events: list[tuple[str, int]],
                     last_complete_period: int, max_age: int):
    if max_age < 0 or not isinstance(last_complete_period, int):
        raise ValueError("age and complete-period watermark must be valid")
    entry = {}
    cohorts = defaultdict(set)
    for member_id, period in enrollments:
        if not member_id or member_id in entry or period > last_complete_period:
            raise ValueError("members need one completed entry period")
        entry[member_id] = period
        cohorts[period].add(member_id)
    if not entry:
        raise ValueError("at least one enrolled member is required")
    returned = defaultdict(set)
    for member_id, period in return_events:
        if (member_id not in entry or period < entry[member_id] or
                period > last_complete_period):
            raise ValueError("return event falls outside the observed member history")
        returned[(entry[member_id], period - entry[member_id])].add(member_id)
    rows = []
    for cohort_period in sorted(cohorts):
        size = len(cohorts[cohort_period])
        cells = [1.0]
        for age in range(1, max_age + 1):
            cells.append(None if cohort_period + age > last_complete_period
                         else len(returned[(cohort_period, age)]) / size)
        rows.append((cohort_period, size, cells))
    return rows

members = [("member-47", 47), ("member-59", 47), ("member-83", 47),
           ("member-97", 48), ("member-131", 48), ("member-149", 49)]
returns = [("member-47", 48), ("member-47", 48), ("member-83", 48),
           ("member-47", 49), ("member-97", 49)]
heatmap = retention_ledger(members, returns, last_complete_period=49, max_age=2)
assert heatmap[0] == (47, 3, [1.0, 2 / 3, 1 / 3])
assert heatmap[1] == (48, 2, [1.0, 1 / 2, None])
assert heatmap[2] == (49, 1, [1.0, None, None])

Performance and operating cost

For E enrollments, A return records, C cohorts and H requested ages, membership construction and event deduplication take O(E + A) expected time; sorting cohort keys takes O(C log C), and cell construction takes O(C·H). The entry and activity sets use O(E + A) space in the worst case, with O(C·H) output cells. Duplicate age-one activity from member-47 still counts once, while the newest cohort's future cells are None rather than zero. Period integers stand for consecutive, fully closed reporting periods; use a calendar-aware key upstream when weeks or months cross time-zone or fiscal boundaries.

Common Mistakes

  • Reassigning a returning member to a new entry cohort.
  • Dividing by the previous period's active members while labeling the result cohort retention.
  • Painting future or partial-period cells as zero percent.
  • Counting duplicate return events as multiple retained users.

Validation drill

Build weekly retention for 47 synthetic signup cohorts with a fixed last-complete-week watermark. Reconcile unique entry IDs, duplicate activity events and cohort sizes; publish age-one and age-four counts as well as rates, and leave all immature cells blank.

title: Autocorrelation plots: align equal-spaced periods before reading lag peaks
summary: Calculate lagged association only over valid pairs, report support by lag and distinguish a seasonal clue from a causal explanation.
body:
Calculate lagged association only over valid pairs, report support by lag and distinguish a seasonal clue from a causal explanation.

A lag must mean the same elapsed time

An autocorrelation plot places lag on the horizontal axis and the association between a series and its own shifted values on the vertical axis. Lag two means two sampling intervals, not merely two available rows. If a daily series skips Tuesday and the values on Monday and Wednesday are adjacent in a database query, treating them as lag one silently changes the elapsed time. Choose a fixed sampling schedule, sort by period, reject duplicates and gaps or apply a separately documented missing-data policy. The simple ledger below requires consecutive integer period IDs and finite measurements. Gap and calendar rules establish the input contract; event-aligned charts answer a different timing question.

Show pair counts, not just spikes

At lag k, only N minus k aligned pairs remain from N complete observations. Large lags therefore have less support, and a dramatic coefficient based on four pairs is fragile. Print the number of pairs beside a selected coefficient or in a companion table. The worked code uses Pearson correlation with means recalculated for each aligned pair set. This is a descriptive lagged Pearson coefficient, not every software package's traditional autocorrelation-function estimator, which may use a full-series mean and normalization. Name the estimator before comparing values across tools. A constant member of a pair set has zero variance, so the coefficient is undefined; display a missing mark instead of a fabricated zero. Small-sample display keeps thin tails visible without overstating them.

Read repetition cautiously

An alternating workload may produce a negative lag-one value and a positive lag-two value. A slow trend can also produce several high positive lag values even without a repeating cycle. A weekly schedule, a changed product mix or an instrumentation reset may create peaks that disappear after appropriate stratification or differencing. Inspect the run chart and known operational calendar before calling a spike seasonality. Correlation at a lag is not evidence that an earlier observation causes a later one. If the goal is forecasting, validate the candidate lag on held-out future periods and avoid using future values while constructing features. Forecast intervals describe predictive uncertainty, while event annotations make causal claims easier to audit.

Treat reference bands as assumptions

A horizontal zero line helps read sign. Statistical confidence bands require a noise model, chosen estimator and a policy for many inspected lags; a generic shaded band is not a universal significance test. Adjacent lag estimates are related, and checking dozens of lags invites chance extremes. Freeze a practical maximum lag based on the question and available pairs, then disclose it. When input values are residuals from a fitted model, describe that fit and its validation window; residual autocorrelation can expose missing structure, but a model trained on the entire evaluation span can hide it. Compare adjacent operational phases on the same vertical scale and keep period count, gap policy and estimator in the export. An export manifest carries the needed calculation details.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, sqrt

def lagged_pearson(readings: list[tuple[int, float]], max_lag: int):
    if len(readings) < 4 or not 1 <= max_lag <= len(readings) - 3:
        raise ValueError("retain at least three pairs at every requested lag")
    periods = [period for period, _ in readings]
    values = [value for _, value in readings]
    if (any(not isinstance(period, int) for period in periods) or
            any(current != previous + 1
                for previous, current in zip(periods, periods[1:])) or
            any(not isfinite(value) for value in values)):
        raise ValueError("readings must be ordered, consecutive and finite")
    coefficients = []
    for lag in range(1, max_lag + 1):
        before, after = values[:-lag], values[lag:]
        count = len(before)
        before_mean = sum(before) / count
        after_mean = sum(after) / count
        centered_before = [value - before_mean for value in before]
        centered_after = [value - after_mean for value in after]
        numerator = sum(left * right for left, right in zip(centered_before,
                                                            centered_after))
        spread_before = sum(value * value for value in centered_before)
        spread_after = sum(value * value for value in centered_after)
        correlation = (numerator / sqrt(spread_before * spread_after)
                       if spread_before and spread_after else None)
        coefficients.append((lag, count, correlation))
    return coefficients

alternating_load = list(zip(range(47, 55), [47.0, 59.0] * 4))
lag_summary = lagged_pearson(alternating_load, 3)
assert lag_summary[0] == (1, 7, -1.0)
assert lag_summary[1] == (2, 6, 1.0)
assert lag_summary[2] == (3, 5, -1.0)
assert lagged_pearson([(47, 83.0), (48, 83.0), (49, 83.0),
                       (50, 83.0)], 1)[0][2] is None

Performance and operating cost

For N readings and K requested lags, each lag builds and scans N minus k paired values, yielding O(N·K) time and O(N + K) extra space, including temporary centered lists and the result. This favors an inspectable short-lag audit over an optimized transform; large K and long series justify a separately tested faster estimator with its own normalization rules. The eight-period alternating example returns minus one at lags one and three, plus one at lag two, and support counts seven, six and five. Constant readings return an undefined coefficient rather than a false zero.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating consecutive database rows as consecutive time periods after a gap.
  • Comparing coefficients from different estimator conventions without naming the method.
  • Calling a high-lag spike seasonality when only a handful of pairs remain.
  • Adding generic significance bands without a noise model or multiple-lag policy.

Validation drill

Take 83 completed daily workload measurements. Audit dates for gaps and duplicates, predeclare seven lags, plot each lagged coefficient with its pair count, then compare the result with a run chart and the known weekly operating schedule.

title: Distribution plots: keep the tail, missing values and bin policy visible
summary: Histograms and quantile summaries answer shape questions that a single mean or trend line cannot settle.
body:
Histograms and quantile summaries answer shape questions that a single mean or trend line cannot settle.

Distinguish populations

Review delay among completed receipts excludes receipts still open. A histogram of completed delays therefore cannot describe the full submission cohort without a censoring policy. State the population and cutoff. Distribution summaries help reveal a long tail, while a separate pending count shows records that do not yet have a delay.

Choose bins deliberately

A histogram with bins of one hour may appear noisy; a bin of one day can conceal a 24-hour service threshold. Fix bin edges across compared periods and label whether the left or right edge is included. Do not auto-bin each channel independently and then compare the resulting bar heights as though the units were identical.

Retain the tail

A rare 47-hour delay can matter more operationally than a high-volume cluster near five hours. If the axis is cropped to show the center, disclose the number above the cap and provide a full-range or quantile companion view. Invalid negative delays should be separated from valid extremes. Axis policy must remain stable across cohorts.

Make a small fixture

Start with delays of 3, 4, 5, 6 and 47 hours. The mean is 13 and the median is 5. A chart that omits the last value while still reporting the original mean is internally inconsistent. Test zero valid observations, one extreme observation and a delayed arrival that changes a closed reporting period.

Implementation

def delay_bins(delays_hours, edges):
    if len(edges) < 2 or edges[0] < 0 or any(left >= right for left, right in zip(edges, edges[1:])):
        raise ValueError("bin edges must increase from a nonnegative start")
    counts = [0] * (len(edges) - 1)
    overflow = 0
    for delay in delays_hours:
        if delay < edges[0]:
            raise ValueError("delay falls below the declared range")
        location = next((index for index, (left, right) in enumerate(zip(edges, edges[1:]))
                         if left <= delay < right), None)
        if location is None:
            overflow += 1
        else:
            counts[location] += 1
    return counts, overflow

Performance and operating cost

This direct bin search costs O(NB) for N observations and B bins, with O(B) output space. A binary search on sorted edges reduces lookup to O(N log B). Store missing and overflow counts separately so a faster renderer cannot erase them.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not compare histograms with different bin edges as if they were identical.
  • Do not trim a valid operational tail without reporting the omitted count.
  • Do not treat an unfinished receipt as a completed zero-hour delay.

title: Box and violin charts: compare groups without inventing density
summary: Keep sample size, quartiles and bandwidth visible when a smoothed shape represents observations.
body:
Keep sample size, quartiles and bandwidth visible when a smoothed shape represents observations.

Begin with observations

A box summarizes a group's quartiles and median; a violin adds an estimated density shape. Neither replaces the sample size. A smooth violin made from seven delivery times can look as confident as one made from seven thousand. Put each group's count beside its label and show individual points for small groups. Distribution and outlier displays explain what the summary hides. First check whether groups cover the same window, unit and eligibility rule. Otherwise the apparent difference may be a cohort change.

Declare the quartile rule

Software packages can interpolate quartiles differently, and whiskers may mean the extrema or a multiple of the interquartile range. State the rule in the chart caption or export record. A point beyond a whisker is not automatically bad data; it is flagged under that rule. If the decision needs the fraction exceeding a service threshold, calculate that fraction directly rather than asking a box to imply it. An empirical CDF answers threshold questions without a smoothing choice.

Treat bandwidth as a parameter

A violin's width depends on a density estimate and its bandwidth. A wide bandwidth can merge two real modes; a narrow one can turn routine noise into several peaks. Compare more than one defensible bandwidth, retain a rug or points, and do not imply that a thin tail continues beyond a physical limit. The mirrored shape is a drawing convention, not a second population. Normalize violin widths by count only if width should carry count. Otherwise make widths equal and show counts separately. Grain and denominator still matter.

Keep groups comparable

Use the same quantitative axis, bandwidth rule and density normalization across groups. Truncating each group to its own range can make spreads seem alike. For latency data, inspect zeros, censored values and caps before estimating density. If the data include repeated readings from the same device, an independent violin discards pairing. A paired view retains it. Supply a text table with each count, median, quartiles and threshold exceedance for readers who cannot use the shape.

Worked contract

def quartile_summary(readings: list[float]) -> dict[str, float | int]:
    from math import isfinite
    if not readings or any(not isfinite(value) for value in readings):
        raise ValueError("readings must be finite and nonempty")
    ordered = sorted(readings)
    def midpoint(values: list[float]) -> float:
        middle = len(values) // 2
        return (values[middle] if len(values) % 2 else
                (values[middle - 1] + values[middle]) / 2)
    middle = len(ordered) // 2
    lower = ordered[:middle]
    upper = ordered[middle + len(ordered) % 2:]
    return {"count": len(ordered), "median": midpoint(ordered),
            "q1": midpoint(lower) if lower else ordered[0],
            "q3": midpoint(upper) if upper else ordered[0]}

depot_latency = quartile_summary([47, 51, 59, 68, 81, 83, 96])
assert depot_latency == {"count": 7, "median": 68, "q1": 51, "q3": 83}

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N observations costs O(N log N) time and O(N) storage for the ordered copy. A chart with G groups repeats this per group; density estimation adds work set by the estimator and evaluation grid. The code declares a median-of-halves quartile convention and handles a one-item group. It does not draw a violin or claim that seven points support a smooth density. Store the exact convention with the exported summary.

Common Mistakes

  • Drawing a smooth violin for a tiny group without points.
  • Comparing boxes whose whiskers use different rules.
  • Treating a flagged point as an invalid measurement.
  • Changing density bandwidth between groups and reading widths as a real difference.

Validation drill

Compare response times for three depots with 7, 47 and 810 records. Print each count, median and quartile rule; draw points for the smallest group, then inspect whether two bandwidth choices alter the visual claim.

title: Axis scales, baselines and labels: prevent a correct number from telling a false story
summary: Axis choices change visual distance, so the scale must match the comparison and be disclosed wherever it changes interpretation.
body:
Axis choices change visual distance, so the scale must match the comparison and be disclosed wherever it changes interpretation.

Use a meaningful baseline

Bar length is read against its baseline. Starting a bar axis at 0.71 can make two completion rates of 0.74 and 0.77 look several times apart. Use zero for ordinary bar lengths and show exact values when a small difference matters. A line chart may use a narrower range to show variation, but the displayed bounds and units must remain obvious.

Inspect transformations

A logarithmic axis can reveal values across orders of magnitude, but equal screen distances then represent equal ratios rather than equal differences. Zero and negative values need an explicit treatment. Never switch an axis to logarithmic merely to fit an outlier, and never compare a linear-panel slope with a log-panel slope as though they share meaning.

Keep category order honest

Sort categories by a documented metric or a stable domain order. If the order changes at each refresh, motion can look like a performance shift when values are steady. Labels should state percent versus percentage points; moving from 74 to 77 percent is a three-point change, not a three-percent relative change. The chart question decides which comparison is primary.

Test presentation rules

Prepare two rates, 0.74 and 0.77, and verify both bars share zero. Then format them as 74.0% and 77.0%. If a narrow view clips labels, retain an accessible text table. Recheck after filtering because an automatic axis may silently rescale and change the apparent difference.

Implementation

def percentage_point_change(previous_rate, current_rate):
    if not all(0 <= rate <= 1 for rate in (previous_rate, current_rate)):
        raise ValueError("rates must be between zero and one")
    return (current_rate - previous_rate) * 100

change_points = percentage_point_change(0.74, 0.77)

Performance and operating cost

Scale formatting is O(M) for M plotted marks. The larger cost is review: test every filter state that changes axis bounds, zero visibility or label collisions. Cache formatted labels only when underlying rate and unit versions match.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not truncate a bar axis without making the baseline explicit.
  • Do not label a percentage-point movement as a relative percent.
  • Do not hide nonpositive observations when using a logarithmic scale.

title: Heatmaps: make missing cells, rates and color domains explicit
summary: Construct a complete matrix and keep unmeasured cells separate from zero-valued measurements.
body:
Construct a complete matrix and keep unmeasured cells separate from zero-valued measurements.

A cell needs two keys and one measure

A heatmap is a matrix of marks whose position comes from two discrete dimensions and whose fill encodes a value. The first decision is the unit of a cell: one depot-day, one product-hour, or one model-class pair. Build the complete expected key grid before coloring it. Otherwise an absent record disappears, compresses the layout, or is mistaken for a low value. A white cell may mean zero, unobserved, unavailable or suppressed; these states require separate labels or patterns. Calendar completeness matters when columns are days.

Rates need their denominators

A defect-rate cell with 4 defects in 8 inspections and another with 40 in 800 inspections should not be interpreted as equally reliable even if their colors reflect 50% and 5%. Carry inspected count into a tooltip, visible annotation, or companion display. If no inspections occurred, the rate is undefined rather than zero. Measure grain determines whether the numerator and denominator belong to the same cell. If filters remove rows, recompute both counts instead of averaging precomputed cell percentages.

Fix the color domain for comparison

An automatically rescaled palette can make the same value change color when the viewer filters a subset. For cross-filter or before-after comparisons, set a stable domain and show its endpoints. A sequential palette fits a nonnegative rate; a diverging palette needs a meaningful center such as zero difference or target variance. Quantile coloring gives bins with similar record counts, not equal numeric widths. Label the bin rule. Accessible encodings add text or pattern cues so the chart still works without color.

Choose ordering deliberately

Alphabetical row order is reproducible, but ordering by a stable baseline can expose patterns. Clustering rows by similarity can reveal structure yet change the question: adjacent rows no longer imply geographic or operational proximity. If an algorithm orders rows, record its input period and freeze the order for comparisons. Keep hidden categories and totals visible. A truncated matrix that shows only the busiest depots is a selected population, not the entire network. Facet-order discipline applies here too.

Test the matrix contract

Include an observed zero, a missing key, a present key with zero exposure, an invalid negative count and a high-rate low-volume cell. Confirm each has a distinct state. Check the matrix against a long-form data table with the same row and column order. On mobile, provide axis labels that remain visible while scrolling; a distant legend is not enough. Exported CSV should retain status, numerator and denominator rather than only a color code.

Worked contract

def inspection_matrix(
    observations: dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[int, int]],
    depots: list[str], days: list[str]
) -> dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[str, float | None, int | None]]:
    expected = {(depot, day) for depot in depots for day in days}
    if len(expected) != len(depots) * len(days) or set(observations) - expected:
        raise ValueError("duplicate labels or unexpected cell")
    grid = {}
    for key in expected:
        if key not in observations:
            grid[key] = ("missing", None, None)
            continue
        defects, inspected = observations[key]
        if not 0 <= defects <= inspected:
            raise ValueError("invalid cell counts")
        grid[key] = ("no-exposure", None, 0) if inspected == 0 else (
            "observed", defects / inspected, inspected)
    return grid

matrix = inspection_matrix(
    {("north", "Mon"): (0, 47), ("north", "Tue"): (0, 0)},
    ["north"], ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"])
assert matrix[("north", "Mon")] == ("observed", 0.0, 47)
assert matrix[("north", "Tue")][0] == "no-exposure"
assert matrix[("north", "Wed")][0] == "missing"

Performance and operating cost

For R row labels, C column labels and M supplied observations, building the expected grid takes O(RC + M) time and O(RC) space. Large sparse matrices should keep sparse storage and generate only visible tiles, but must still represent missing cells and axis positions correctly. The demonstration returns status, rate and denominator; a production export should also retain the numerator and source snapshot. Color scaling and rendering add work proportional to visible cells, not merely to supplied observations.

Common Mistakes

  • Assigning the same white fill to an observed zero and an absent cell.
  • Changing the color domain after filtering without warning the reader.
  • Averaging cell percentages instead of recomputing counts for a new group.
  • Sorting rows by one selected day, then describing the layout as a stable geographic order.

Validation drill

Build a depot-by-day inspection matrix with 6 depots and 17 days. Insert one missing cell, one zero-exposure cell and one observed zero. Verify their states in both chart legend and exported data.

title: Interactive dashboards: recompute cohorts after linked filters
summary: Make selections compose predictably, recalculate numerators and denominators, and expose the active state.
body:
Make selections compose predictably, recalculate numerators and denominators, and expose the active state.

A selection changes the population

Linked filtering lets a selection in one view constrain another. Clicking a depot, brushing a date range or choosing a channel changes the cohort behind every plotted metric. The interaction contract must specify whether filters combine with AND or OR, whether a second click toggles, and whether an empty selection means all or none. Show active filters in text and offer a clear reset. Dashboard provenance needs the same filter state that the user sees; otherwise a shared screenshot cannot be reproduced.

Recompute base counts

A precomputed overall completion percentage cannot simply be filtered and averaged. Reapply the filter to eligible records, then sum timely and eligible counts for the selected cohort. If a record appears in both a status log and an order table, deduplicate to the declared unit before counting. Grain and denominator rules are the invariant under interaction. A filtered group with zero eligible records should display an undefined rate and zero denominator, not a zero-percent success rate.

Synchronize every view

When a brush narrows a chart, its companion count, data table, map and export must use the same selected IDs or query predicate. Some dashboards filter the marks but leave the headline KPI unfiltered; users then compare incompatible populations. Carry one normalized state object and one data-version token into each query. If a backend response arrives after the user changes filters again, discard the stale response instead of replacing a newer view. A request ID or abort signal can enforce this. Large-series rendering may be approximate, but filter semantics must remain exact.

Make selection discoverable and reversible

Hover-only behavior hides controls from touch and keyboard users. Provide visible filter chips, keyboard-operable controls, focus cues and a readable selection summary. Color should not be the sole indication of selected marks. A reset should restore the documented default and preserve the date or snapshot policy, not silently switch to today's data. Accessible chart controls include data values outside the plotted canvas. Keep the browser back button or a shareable query state when deep analysis paths matter.

Test the state machine

Exercise no filters, one filter, two intersecting filters, mutually exclusive filters, a zero-eligible result, and rapid filter changes. Compare chart, KPI and export row counts for each state. For a selected region and channel, check that removing one chip broadens the cohort only along that dimension. Record the expected query predicate alongside a screenshot in a release test. If the chart is based on sampled or aggregated data, do not use a pixel brush to imply record-level exactness unless the backend can resolve it.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReviewRecord:
    receipt_id: str
    region: str
    channel: str
    eligible: bool
    timely: bool

def filtered_completion(records: list[ReviewRecord],
                        regions: set[str], channels: set[str]
                        ) -> tuple[int, int, float | None]:
    if len({record.receipt_id for record in records}) != len(records):
        raise ValueError("duplicate receipt identity")
    selected = [record for record in records
                if (not regions or record.region in regions)
                and (not channels or record.channel in channels)
                and record.eligible]
    if any(record.timely and not record.eligible for record in records):
        raise ValueError("timely receipt cannot be ineligible")
    timely = sum(record.timely for record in selected)
    eligible = len(selected)
    return timely, eligible, timely / eligible if eligible else None

receipts = [ReviewRecord("r-47", "north", "web", True, True),
            ReviewRecord("r-81", "north", "store", True, False),
            ReviewRecord("r-94", "south", "web", True, True)]
assert filtered_completion(receipts, {"north"}, {"web"}) == (1, 1, 1.0)
assert filtered_completion(receipts, {"south"}, {"store"}) == (0, 0, None)

Performance and operating cost

For N records, duplicate validation and filtering take O(N) expected time and O(N) temporary space in this direct version; the selected list can be avoided with streaming counters to use O(N) identity state and O(1) additional cohort state. For a remote dashboard, query cost and transfer volume usually dominate. Cache only by normalized filters, authorization context and data version. Never reuse a cached result across tenants or revisions merely because the visible filter chips match.

Common Mistakes

  • Filtering colored marks while leaving headline metrics on the full population.
  • Averaging cached percentages after a filter instead of summing base counts.
  • Treating an empty cohort as a measured zero-percent rate.
  • Letting an older network response overwrite the result of a newer selection.

Connect a weekly trend, region bar chart and completion KPI. Test six filter states and verify the same eligible count in the chart tooltip, KPI, table and CSV export for each state.

title: Funnel charts: hold the cohort still before calculating conversion
summary: Reconcile stage populations and time windows before publishing conversion rates or drop-off shapes.
body:
Reconcile stage populations and time windows before publishing conversion rates or drop-off shapes.

A funnel is a population claim

Each stage should represent the same entrants moving through a declared sequence within a stated observation window. Counting every visit at stage one and only new users at stage two mixes populations. Define entrant ID, entry date, stage completion event and maximum allowed delay. Then count unique entrants reaching each stage. Grain and denominator rules make rates reproducible. Keep re-entries and repeated events explicit, since deduplication changes every step.

Distinguish step and overall rates

A step conversion divides the current stage count by the immediately previous count. An overall conversion divides by the entry count. If 470 entrants reach review and 188 reach approval out of 810 starts, approval's step rate is 188/470 or 40 percent; overall approval is 188/810 or about 23.2 percent. Both are useful, but a chart with unlabeled percentages is ambiguous. Show count and denominator beside each rate. Composition charts face the same denominator trap.

Late arrivals can make a false drop

A current-week cohort has had less time to reach later stages than an older cohort. Wait until the conversion window has matured or mark rates provisional with a maturity cutoff. Do not compare a mature 29-day cohort with one observed for two days. Provisional-period labels make this visible. If stages can be skipped or revisited, a strict funnel loses information; use a transition or flow view instead. Flow conservation applies when exits and skips matter.

Audit monotonicity

For a strict cohort funnel, counts cannot rise as stages advance. An increase signals duplicate counting, a changed filter, late data or a non-strict process. Do not clamp bars to make the chart look right. Inspect raw identities and stage timestamps. Segment filters should use a stable entry-time property; filtering later by a property acquired after conversion can bias the chart toward successful entrants. Linked filters must preserve the entry cohort. Export stage order, window, counts and both rate definitions.

Worked contract

def strict_funnel(stage_members: list[tuple[str, set[str]]]
                  ) -> list[tuple[str, int, float | None, float | None]]:
    if not stage_members or len({name for name, _ in stage_members}) != len(stage_members):
        raise ValueError("stages must be named and unique")
    entrants = stage_members[0][1]
    previous = entrants
    result = []
    for stage_name, members in stage_members:
        if not members <= previous:
            raise ValueError("stage contains non-eligible entrants")
        result.append((stage_name, len(members),
                       len(members) / len(previous) if previous else None,
                       len(members) / len(entrants) if entrants else None))
        previous = members
    return result

stages = [("start", {"u47", "u59", "u71", "u83"}),
          ("review", {"u47", "u59", "u71"}),
          ("approve", {"u47", "u71"})]
funnel = strict_funnel(stages)
assert funnel[-1] == ("approve", 2, 2 / 3, 2 / 4)

Performance and operating cost

For S stages and total M stored membership IDs, subset checks and counts use O(M) expected time with hash sets and O(S) output space beyond the supplied sets. Persisting full ID sets can be costly; a warehouse may compute stage membership with distinct keys and checked joins. The example assumes a strict nested sequence and says nothing about timestamps or cohort maturity; enforce those earlier in the data pipeline.

Common Mistakes

  • Mixing sessions at one stage with unique people at another.
  • Using a previous-stage denominator while labeling it overall conversion.
  • Comparing mature and immature cohorts without a cutoff.
  • Forcing increasing counts down to the prior stage instead of fixing the event model.

Validation drill

Build a three-stage funnel for 810 entrants with a 29-day window. Report step and overall rates, then inject a skipped-stage user and explain why strict validation rejects that path.

Show the independent count

Two channels can both report a 75 percent completion rate, yet one may have 12 receipts and another 12,000. Put eligible counts near marks or in an accessible companion table. If customers submit repeated receipts, the independent count may be customers rather than rows. Cluster resampling keeps those observations together.

Choose an interval contract

Specify the estimator, interval construction, confidence level and sampling unit. Error bars from an independent-row formula are misleading when assignments or outcomes cluster by reviewer. A confidence interval describes a repeated-sampling procedure; it is not a probability distribution over the displayed fixed rate. Coverage requires a valid observation process.

Separate overlap from decision

Overlapping intervals do not by themselves establish that a difference is absent, and nonoverlap is not a universal experiment test. If the task is to compare channels, calculate and display an interval for the difference under the study design. Pair this with practical limits: a two-point change may matter only above a declared volume or cost threshold.

Handle thin groups

A filter may leave one receipt or none. Use a visible “insufficient data” state rather than a narrow-looking point with absent error bars. Check that each interval is within the metric domain and that chart tooling does not clip it without notice. Keep the raw numerator and denominator available for audit.

Implementation

def interval_mark(point_rate, lower_rate, upper_rate, eligible_count):
    if eligible_count < 2:
        return {"state": "insufficient_data", "eligible_count": eligible_count}
    if not 0 <= lower_rate <= point_rate <= upper_rate <= 1:
        raise ValueError("invalid rate interval")
    return {"state": "measured", "point": point_rate,
            "lower": lower_rate, "upper": upper_rate, "eligible_count": eligible_count}

Performance and operating cost

Formatting M intervals is O(M) time and space. Interval estimation may be much more expensive, especially when resampling clusters; calculate it in a versioned data job and render the stored estimate with its construction metadata.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not draw error bars without naming their meaning.
  • Do not use receipt count as the independent sample size when customers repeat.
  • Do not interpret overlapping intervals as a complete test of a difference.

title: Time-series charts: distinguish missing days, zeros and provisional periods
summary: Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.
body:
Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.

A line implies continuity

A time-series chart maps measurements to ordered instants or calendar periods. Connecting two observed points across an unobserved day implies a path that was never measured. A recorded zero is different: it says the instrument or process observed the period and counted none. Store both the period key and an observation-status field before drawing the line. The observation calendar defines which periods were expected. Use a visible break, hollow mark, or separate missingness strip when a period has no measurement; do not silently replace it with zero.

Name the two clocks

Operational data often has an event timestamp and a processing timestamp. A refund received late may belong to Tuesday's customer cohort but be visible only on Thursday's dashboard. Choose the clock that answers the chart's question and label it in the axis or subtitle. When bucketing timestamps into local days, choose one time zone and convert before taking the date. Daylight-saving changes make a local day shorter or longer than 24 hours in some regions. An elapsed-duration chart should use instants; a calendar-day chart should use dates in the declared zone.

Mark provisional periods

A current day is incomplete even when its count is known so far. Drawing it with the same line and scale as closed days invites a false decline. Carry a finalized flag from the data source, and either exclude the open interval or render it with a different stroke and an explicit as-of time. Late corrections can reopen an earlier point, so the chart's data-version label matters. A reader must know whether yesterday is final, not only whether the plotting job ran.

Protect the comparison

Never join lines across a product outage, a changed population, or a denominator change without an annotation or split. Keep the y-axis unit and calculation stable across the displayed range. If one week contains 42, 47 and 51 eligible cases while the next has a different intake rule, raw counts compare different populations. The aggregation contract should produce both numerator and denominator where a rate is intended. A moving average may reduce noise, but its window, edge behavior and missing-day policy must be stated.

Check the drawn output

Test an interior missing day, an observed zero, an incomplete final day, a late revision, and a daylight-saving boundary for the region being displayed. Confirm that hover text, downloadable data and the axis all use the same period key. A chart-library setting that connects nulls can undo a carefully prepared missingness contract. Inspect the rendered image, not only the input array. The text alternative should report the gap and the as-of timestamp too.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta

def complete_daily_series(observed: dict[date, int],
                          start: date, end: date) -> list[tuple[date, int | None]]:
    if end < start or any(count < 0 for count in observed.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid date range or count")
    if any(day < start or day > end for day in observed):
        raise ValueError("observation outside display range")
    return [(start + timedelta(days=offset),
             observed.get(start + timedelta(days=offset)))
            for offset in range((end - start).days + 1)]

points = complete_daily_series(
    {date(2026, 8, 11): 47, date(2026, 8, 13): 0},
    date(2026, 8, 11), date(2026, 8, 13))
assert [count for _, count in points] == [47, None, 0]

Performance and operating cost

For D expected periods and O observed keys, validation plus calendar completion takes O(D + O) time and O(D) output space. The code assumes an already chosen calendar zone and one authoritative count per day. Converting event timestamps and resolving duplicates belong upstream. For a long history, query only the visible interval, and keep finalization state beside each point; creating a million empty periods in a browser is a serving error, not a charting technique.

Common Mistakes

  • Converting an unobserved period into zero and drawing a continuous line.
  • Bucketing by server time zone while labeling the axis with the user's local dates.
  • Treating today's partial count as a completed daily value.
  • Using a rolling average without showing its window and missing-period rule.

Validation drill

Plot a 29-day refund series with one observed zero, two missing days and a provisional last day. Export the period keys and states, then verify that the line breaks only where observation is absent.

title: Event-aligned charts: choose a baseline before comparing trajectories
summary: Align observations to a real event, retain calendar context and make missing periods explicit.
body:
Align observations to a real event, retain calendar context and make missing periods explicit.

Event time is not calendar time

An event-aligned chart puts each subject's event at relative time zero. This lets a reader compare trajectories before and after events that occurred on different calendar dates. Store the actual event timestamp as well as the relative offset; otherwise seasonality, outages and policy changes disappear. Specify whether an offset means elapsed hours, calendar days or complete reporting periods. Time-series period rules are essential when the event occurs late in a day or across a daylight-saving change.

Fix the baseline rule

A common display subtracts each subject's pre-event value or divides by it. These produce different shapes and units. Select the baseline window before inspecting outcomes, report how many valid observations contributed to it, and reject a percentage change when the baseline is zero. If one subject has only one pre-event measurement and another has 47, their aligned curves carry different reliability. Denominator and grain rules should stay visible with the chart. Plot absolute values alongside normalized values when the magnitude of the original series matters.

Missing is not flat

Do not fill missing pre-event days with the baseline or connect a line across an unobserved outage without a marker. A cohort average at relative day five may use fewer subjects than at day one because follow-up ends; show the contributing count by offset. Attrition can make a trend look like improvement. Small-sample uncertainty belongs near sparse tails, and forecast intervals must not be substituted for missing actual observations.

The line does not prove an effect

A change at time zero can reflect selection into the event, a concurrent intervention, regression to the mean or ordinary seasonality. An annotation identifies timing, not causality. Compare a relevant untreated group or a pre-specified benchmark if the decision requires an effect estimate, and state the assumptions of that comparison. Annotation and causal-claim boundaries apply here. Export subject ID, event date, relative offset, original value, baseline window, normalized value and eligibility state so every plotted line can be reconstructed.

Worked contract

from datetime import date
from math import isfinite

def event_aligned_change(event_day: date, observations: dict[date, float],
                         baseline_days: tuple[date, ...]
                        ) -> list[tuple[int, float, float]]:
    if not baseline_days or len(set(baseline_days)) != len(baseline_days):
        raise ValueError("baseline days must be distinct")
    if any(day >= event_day or day not in observations for day in baseline_days):
        raise ValueError("baseline must be observed before the event")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in observations.values()):
        raise ValueError("observations must be finite")
    baseline = sum(observations[day] for day in baseline_days) / len(baseline_days)
    return sorted(((day - event_day).days, value, value - baseline)
                  for day, value in observations.items())

incident_counts = {
    date(2026, 10, 5): 47, date(2026, 10, 6): 59,
    date(2026, 10, 8): 38, date(2026, 10, 9): 35,
}
aligned = event_aligned_change(
    date(2026, 10, 7), incident_counts,
    (date(2026, 10, 5), date(2026, 10, 6)),
)
assert aligned == [(-2, 47, -6), (-1, 59, 6), (1, 38, -15), (2, 35, -18)]
assert all(offset != 0 for offset, _, _ in aligned)

Performance and operating cost

For N observations and B baseline days, validation and averaging take O(N+B) time; sorting relative periods takes O(N log N) time and O(N) output space. The function leaves missing event day zero absent instead of inventing a value. Calendar dates are appropriate only when day-level reporting is the contract; intraday events need zoned timestamps and a declared binning method. Subtracting a baseline describes change, not a causal estimate.

Common Mistakes

  • Discarding calendar dates after alignment and losing concurrent-event context.
  • Choosing a favorable baseline window after seeing the result.
  • Drawing a continuous line over days with no observations.
  • Calling a post-event change proof that the event caused it.

Validation drill

Align 81 facilities around a maintenance intervention. Show each facility's baseline window and post-event coverage, then recompute the cohort curve using only facilities observed through day 14.

title: Forecast fan charts: label interval meaning and forecast horizon
summary: Separate observed history from forecasts and keep coverage claims attached to their method.
body:
Separate observed history from forecasts and keep coverage claims attached to their method.

A band needs a named quantity

A shaded region around a forecast could show uncertainty in an estimated mean, uncertainty for a future individual outcome, or a range of scenarios. These are different claims. A future-observation prediction interval is usually wider than an interval for the mean under the same model assumptions. Label the target, coverage level and calibration period. Uncertainty displays should also expose sample size and unstable estimates. Color alone must not carry the difference between observed and projected values.

Mark the boundary

Draw the last observed time as a visible boundary and use a different line style for forecasts. A continuous line through that boundary can make modeled values look measured. Do not fill missing observed dates with predictions and call the whole line history. Time-series gap rules still govern the observed segment. State whether the first future period is a complete day, week or fiscal interval, especially when a dashboard refreshes mid-period.

Nested bands need checks

A fan chart may show 50, 80 and 95 percent intervals. At each horizon, narrower bands must sit inside wider ones. The lower bound may fall and the upper bound may rise as coverage increases. Check containment in the data before rendering. Wider horizons often have wider uncertainty, but that shape is not guaranteed for every conditioned model or bounded target. Never widen bands by hand for appearance. The export should retain interval definition, model version and generation time.

Backtest the claim

If an interval claims 80 percent coverage, compare past issued intervals with realized values at a fixed forecast horizon and documented window. Count misses alongside nominal coverage. A recent shock or measurement change can break earlier calibration. An 80 percent band is not a promise that exactly eight of every ten future points must land inside it; coverage is assessed across repeated forecasts under stated conditions. Event annotations can mark changed processes without proving their cause.

Worked contract

def validate_fan_rows(rows: list[dict]) -> None:
    previous_horizon = -1
    for row in rows:
        horizon = row["horizon"]
        if not isinstance(horizon, int) or horizon <= previous_horizon:
            raise ValueError("horizons must increase")
        previous_horizon = horizon
        center = row["forecast"]
        inner = row["interval_50"]
        outer = row["interval_80"]
        if not (outer[0] <= inner[0] <= center <= inner[1] <= outer[1]):
            raise ValueError("intervals must nest around forecast")

issued_forecast = [
    {"horizon": 1, "forecast": 81,
     "interval_50": (75, 87), "interval_80": (68, 94)},
    {"horizon": 2, "forecast": 83,
     "interval_50": (74, 92), "interval_80": (62, 104)},
]
validate_fan_rows(issued_forecast)
assert issued_forecast[1]["interval_80"][1] == 104

Performance and operating cost

Validation scans H horizons in O(H) time and O(1) additional space. Rendering nested bands scales with horizons times interval levels. The check verifies ordering and containment only; it cannot establish empirical coverage, calibration or model quality. Finite numeric values and exact time-zone handling also need validation at the source boundary before a production forecast is issued.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling a mean-confidence band a future-observation prediction interval.
  • Drawing forecast points with the same style as measurements.
  • Allowing an 80 percent band to cross inside its 50 percent band.
  • Claiming nominal coverage without checking past issued forecasts against outcomes.

Validation drill

Issue 47 weekly forecasts with saved 50 and 80 percent bounds. Mark the observed-to-forecast boundary, validate every nested interval, and report realized coverage at horizons one and four separately.
